en: The Buddha’s *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of Definitive Meaning*,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial and Acting Director of the Court of State Protocol,
Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, under Imperial Decree.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"You should now know this: any bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the conduct associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) must understand all phenomena as they truly are, and in whatever they do, remain free from all signs."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra joined his palms in reverent salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the World-Honored One has said, regarding those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to practice the conduct associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), how should they understand the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena?”
"How does one become free from signs regarding all that is done?
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra!..."

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas desire to fulfill the superior practices associated with aspiration, and regarding all phenomena remain free from the marks of activity, they should understand that all phenomena abide in non-abiding; thus, they will be able to fulfill the superior practices associated with aspiration.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving within all phenomena, there is no giver, no object given, and no recipient of the gift; if they act in this way, they are able to fulfill the perfection of giving."

Furthermore, for one who practices the various dharmas of the precepts, there is no one who upholds them, nothing that is upheld, and no act of initiation; if it is thus, one is able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

Furthermore, one who practices the dharma of patience remains unmoved amidst all phenomena and is free from all conditioned activity; if one is thus, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, one should practice with diligence within the context of corresponding conduct; if one is neither weary in body nor mind, and remains free from the notion of exertion, then one will be able to fulfill the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, being without distraction regarding all phenomena and free from the marks of attainment—if one is thus, one will be able to fulfill the perfection of concentration (samādhipāramitā).

“Śāriputra! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas wish to dwell in accordance with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should bring to fulfillment the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.”

Furthermore, one contemplates the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness; the dharmas of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive abidings, and the nine perceptions.
What are called the nine perceptions?

They are: the perception of internal phenomena, the perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a discolored corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, the perception of a burned corpse, and the perception of a corpse devoid of food.
These are called the nine perceptions of phenomena.

Furthermore, there are the perception of recollecting the Buddha, the perception of recollecting the Dharma, and the perception of recollecting the Sangha; the perceptions of recollecting ethical discipline, generosity, and the devas;
the perception of being free from afflictions; the perception of recollecting arising and ceasing; and the perception of recollecting impermanence and suffering.
The perception of non-self; the perception of all worlds as being non-ultimate;
the perception of the knowledge of suffering, the perception of the knowledge of the origin, the perception of the knowledge of cessation, and the perception of the knowledge of the path;

the perception of the knowledge of exhaustion, the perception of the knowledge of non-arising, the perception of the knowledge of phenomena, the perception of the knowledge of non-self, the perception of the knowledge of conjunction, and the perception of the knowledge of reality as it is—thus he speaks.
The notion of conceptual discrimination, the notion of being free from linguistic conceptual discrimination;

the notion of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the notion of the faculty of "knowing," and the notion of the faculty of "one who has known"; the notion of impurity, the notion of purity; the notions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
the notion of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*); the notion of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); and the notion of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
The perception of the five supernormal powers, the perception of the six perfections, the perception of the seven stages of mental abiding, the perception of the eight qualities of a great person,
the perception of the nine abodes of sentient beings, the perception of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the perception of the eighteen unique qualities,
the perception of great loving-kindness, the perception of great compassion, and even the perception of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge— within these...
Regarding such dharmas as these, one should form such a conception.
Furthermore, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who desire to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*) should contemplate the *prajñāpāramitā* according to reality.

Furthermore, if one wishes to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, to thoroughly comprehend the mental activities and characteristics of all sentient beings, and to eliminate all the various defilements of all sentient beings, one should practice the sublime conduct associated with the perfection of wisdom.
“Śāriputra! Just as I have previously explained the gateways of conceptualization regarding all phenomena, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this manner.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), what dharmas should they sever?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! One who cultivates the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should eliminate ten kinds of doubt.
What are these ten?

These are: doubt regarding existence, doubt regarding non-existence, doubt regarding the differentiation of phenomena, doubt regarding disparagement, doubt regarding a single phenomenon, doubt regarding multiple phenomena, doubt regarding identity and difference, superior-grade doubt, doubt regarding names, and doubt regarding the meaning of names.
These ten doubts should be eliminated and severed. If this is so, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe anything at all among all marks (*nimitta*).
Because no mark is observed, names (*nāman*) are also not observed;

the *prajñāpāramitā* is not observed, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not observed, form (*rūpa*) is not observed, and feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all not observed.
Why is this? The intrinsic nature of form is empty, because emptiness is devoid of intrinsic nature.
The essence of form is itself emptiness; apart from form, there is no separate emptiness. The essence of emptiness is itself form; apart from emptiness, there is no separate form.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because it is called "discrimination. "Śāriputra!..."
One should know that the intrinsic nature of form is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure.

Its name is also not a conditioned phenomenon; it is free from all doubt and delusion, coming from nowhere and abiding nowhere. It arises in accordance with reality, for it is detached from the three periods of time.
Form is thus; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.

Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe any names or signs. Because there is nothing observed, there is no entering. One who does not enter is able to fulfill the sublime practice associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha spoke this definitive Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom.
